transcript:
Header: 2026-03-04 16:00 UTC | Duration: 55m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Lena (Redwood AE), Rahul (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE - infra), Mark Liu (StratusAI Head of ML), Sofia (Infra), Daniel (CTO), Erin (PM)

[00:00] Lena: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh let's do quick intros and then we'll jump into tail latency stuff, we know Stratus has tight sgos for interactive assistant so want to focus on p95/p99.
[00:12] Mark: yeah thanks lena, im Mark, we run a multi-tenant inference platform for our assistants, target 200-300ms p95 for short queries, p99 ideally < 500ms but that's been the trouble.
[00:26] Rahul: cool; quick note on agenda — we'll run through p95/p99 sources, show examples from our dedicated infra, then discuss streaming vs non-streaming and how KV cache and batching interplay.
[00:38] Sofia: quick ask — we are onboarding Redwood Private (VPC) eval, so network hops and NAT behavior are a big unknown for us.
[00:45] Priya: perfect, we'll call out typical network path impacts — VPC peering, NAT, cross-AZ.

[02:05] James: first thing, high level root causes of tail latency: queueing/backpressure at the batching layer, cold KV cache misses, kernel-level jitter on GPUs, and network retries. also OS-level interrupts and GC in orchestration can surface.
[02:25] Mark: we mostly see spikes when sessions have longer context or when we have concurrent requests hitting different models. also spikey traffic from user bursts.

[05:10] Rahul: demo numbers from Redwood Dedicated (internal): for a 2k token context, non-streaming generation p95 ~ 220ms, p99 ~ 520ms on A10G try. streaming mode reduces observable tail for perceived latency because first-token is fast but p99 for full-response completion still shows similar tail due to finalization and KV flush.
[05:40] Erin: can you explain that — streaming reduces tail latency? I thought it fixes tail for interactive apps.
[05:48] Rahul: good question — streaming primarily helps perceived latency (time-to-first-byte). But if your p99 SLO is defined as time-to-last-byte or overall request completion, streaming doesn't hide backend tail sources like cache misses or long queueing. streaming gives partial mitigation for UX but not for total compute tail.

[08:00] Sofia: network hops — our architecture will place Redwood Private in our VPC and we expect cross-AZ traffic, possibly through NAT GW. which pieces add the most latency?
[08:15] Priya: typical path: customer app -> ELB -> NAT/Transit -> Redwood Private node. Cross-AZ adds ~1-3ms on AWS typically; NAT gateway can add 5-15ms when under load. But the big tail often comes from internal queueing at the GPU host when bursts exceed batch window.

[10:35] Mark: about KV cache — sometimes we see a big jump in latency when cache is cold, is that quantized? what's the difference between prefix cache and kv cache?
[10:52] Rahul: quick defs: prefix cache stores tokenized prefix embeddings so you avoid re-computing early layers; KV cache is the autoregressive key/value cache kept per sequence to avoid recomputing attention states. Cold prefix or kv cache misses cause extra compute to rebuild states and increase latency. We also have eager warming strategies.
[11:18] Mark: ok so cache warming is critical. how do you warm cache at scale with multi-tenant workloads?
[11:26] Rahul: options: proactive warming (precompute hot prefixes), sticky routing (route same session to same host to preserve KV), and fast shared prefix cache techniques. tradeoff is memory footprint and staleness. we support sticky sessions in Dedicated/Private to reduce misses.

[13:50] James: batching strategy — continuous batching vs fixed-window batching. continuous batching reduces average latency and increases throughput but can create long tails for single-request low concurrency scenarios. fixed-window batching yields predictable batch sizes but can add base latency equal to window. auto-balance policy picks based on request distribution.
[14:30] Sofia: can users configure the batching policy in Private? we need deterministic latency for contracts.
[14:36] Priya: yes — Private exposes per-route batching config: batch_max_size, batch_timeout_ms, and a preferred_policy (low_latency|high_throughput). You can pin small batch sizes and low timeout for strict latency.

[17:05] Rahul: quantization — int8/4bit quant reduces memory and can improve throughput but sometimes increases p99 because of dequant/requant overheads and different kernel paths. the wins are model and hardware dependent. for some transformer kernels, int8 has faster matmul but slower softmax kernels if not optimized.
[17:40] Mark: do you have numbers for small chat models?
[17:45] Rahul: example: Llama2-13B -> fp16 p95 180ms p99 380ms; int8-quant p95 160ms p99 430ms on same node; so p99 worsened in that test due to a slower kernel path on tail batches. we recommend per-model perf profiling before fleet-wide quant.

[20:10] Erin: streaming vs non-streaming benchmarks — do you recommend switching modes dynamically?
[20:20] Rahul: yes — route by request importance. time-sensitive assistant responses can use streaming to get first token fast; batch long-form generation in non-streaming for cost. Redwood routing policies can fallback: if Dedicated is saturated, route to hosted variant with different cost/latency profile.

[22:00] Mark: what about network retries and observability? we need to trace p99 origins.
[22:08] James: we instrument per-token timings: tokenization, kv-read, matmul, softmax, token emit; plus queue time and network egress/ingress. we capture percentiles and heatmaps. We'll share a sample trace CSV.

[25:30] Transcript artifact glitch: Speaker 1 vs Rahul occasionally — automated labels off a little so transcription has errors.

[26:00] Sofia: real world issue — we saw a p99 spike that correlated with a backup job saturating disks on infra hosts. how does Redwood isolate IO?
[26:15] Priya: Private deploy recommended: use local NVMe per GPU host for model artifacts, isolate backups to a separate storage tier, and use cgroups and node-level QoS to limit IO. Also schedulers can preempt lower-priority workloads.

[28:40] Mark: curious about cross-AZ tail — we saw sporadic 200ms spikes when requests route to different AZs during autoscale. how to mitigate?
[28:52] Rahul: prefer AZ-affinity for sticky sessions; use local warm pools; and enable cross-AZ fallback only for availability. Also monitor for transient routing changes from LB which can create TCP teardowns causing spikes.

[31:12] Erin: any suggestions for tests we should run?
[31:18] Rahul: recommended benchmark matrix: 1) baseline small queries (<=64 toks) streaming and non-streaming for p50/p95/p99; 2) long-context tests (2k-4k tokens) cold and warmed KV; 3) bursty concurrent arrival pattern (Poisson) to quantify queueing tail; 4) network path emulation: add 10/50ms of synthetic hop to emulate cross-region. we'll provide harness and scripts.

[34:50] Mark: how quickly can we get a POC on-prem? our infra team wants to validate VPC-less deployment and measure p99.
[34:58] Lena: we can run a Private trial in your lab; typical timeline 2-3 weeks for initial pack + 1 week run. we'll need access to topology and tokenization samples.

[37:20] Priya: one more gotcha — garbage collection and python worker spikes if using containers with many sidecar processes. go lean on systemd or use lightweight runtimes and monitor syscalls.

[39:00] James: another tail cause — model loading when requests hit a cold shard. solutions: keep hot shard pool or lazy load with fast NVMe copy.

[41:55] Sofia: security question — will enabling KV cache sharing leak state across tenants?
[42:05] Rahul: we never share per-tenant KV across tenants. prefix share only applies to public prefixes and sanitized prompts. Dedicated/Private give tenant isolation; Private can integrate with your KMS. We'll send the security docs.

[44:30] Mark: let's talk SLOs — if we define p99 < 500ms for short queries, what's reasonable staging config?
[44:42] Rahul: start with low batch sizes, enable sticky routing, pre-warm hot prefixes, and measure. It's common to accept slightly higher cost to hit strict p99. We'll provide cost vs latency curves.

[47:10] Erin: any tuning knobs you recommend for quant and batching together?
[47:18] Rahul: tune batch_timeout_ms down for int8 if you see kernel variance; use smaller batch_max_size for strict p99. Also profile kernel latencies under quantized path — if a particular kernel regresses, consider mixed precision for that op.

[50:00] Action recap by Lena: Rahul to run benchmarks (streaming vs non-streaming, warmed/cold KV, quant vs fp16) and share traces; Lena to send security packet and pricing; Sofia to send request distribution and sample prompts. Proposed POC week of 2026-03-22.

[52:30] Daniel: thanks all, sounds good. any blockers?
[52:36] Mark: none, just want clear measurement plan.

[54:00] Lena: great thanks everyone; we'll follow up with calendar invites and the benchmark harness.

End of recording.
notes: Transcript includes occasional speaker labeling issues and minor transcription artifacts (common with Fireflies exports). Shared artifacts referenced: perf-harness.csv, security_packet_v2.pdf, pricing-dedicated.xlsx (will be shared by Lena).
